title: Employee Salary Growth Over Time
description:
For each salary record, show the employee's previous salary and the change amount. Records with no previous salary (the employee's first record) should show `NULL` for both `prev_salary` and `salary_change`.

**Table: salary_history** — `id`, `employee_id`, `salary`, `effective_date`

Output columns: `employee_id`, `effective_date`, `salary`, `prev_salary`, `salary_change`. Order by `employee_id`, `effective_date`.
solution_sql: SELECT employee_id, effective_date, salary, LAG(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY employee_id ORDER BY effective_date) AS prev_salary, salary - LAG(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY employee_id ORDER BY effective_date) AS salary_change FROM salary_history ORDER BY employee_id, effective_date;

test_cases.description: 11 total salary records; first record per employee has NULL prev_salary and NULL salary_change

hints: Use LAG(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY employee_id ORDER BY effective_date) to fetch the previous salary.
The salary_change is simply salary - LAG(salary). When there is no previous row, LAG returns NULL and the subtraction also yields NULL.
Employee 2 shows a negative salary_change (pay cut from 45000 to 42000).
explanation: LAG() with PARTITION BY employee_id looks back one row within each employee's history (ordered by effective_date). Employee 1 grew from 50K→55K→60K (+5K each time). Employee 2 took a pay cut (45K→42K, change = -3K). Employee 4 has only one record so prev_salary is NULL. The subtraction propagates NULL automatically.
